newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea delays privatisation, cites weak market.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea delays privatisation, cites weak market.

text.p: A slump in South Korea's stock market has forced the government to delay plans to privatise four big state-run corporations, the finance ministry said on Friday.

Another reason for freezing plans to sell stakes in Korea Gas Corp, Korea Tobacco & Ginseng Corp, Korea Telecom Corp and Korea Heavy Industries & Construction Corp was fears that they could be snapped up by the country's private business conglomerates, a senior ministry official said.
"Given the current depression of the stock market, it will be difficult to sell a large amount of government stock," said Suh Seung-il, director of the ministry's treasury bureau.
The stock market is now down about 22 percent from its high of 986.84 in May.
President Kim Young-sam announced a sweeping privatisation programme after he took power in 1993.
Since then, however, the government has launched an effort to curb the concentration of economic power in the hands of the giant private groups, known as chaebol.

Korea Gas Corp and Korea Heavy Industries & Construction Corp were set to be privatised in 1995, while the Korea Tobacco & Ginseng Corp -- the state liquor and cigarette monopoly -- was to be handed over to the private sector in 1998.
"When we ultimately sell stakes in those companies, we will prevent the chaebol from taking a controlling stake by limiting the ownership," said Suh.
He gave no new timetable.

The government owns 100 percent of Korea Tobacco & Ginseng, has a direct stake of 51 percent in Korea Gas, an 80 percent holding in Korea Telecom and a major stake in Korea Heavy Industries through two state-run banks.
The government has privatised 16 companies and merged five firms since 1993. Under the privatisation programme it intended to privatise 58 companies and merge 10 firms with other state-run companies.
Suh denied the government was backing away from privatisation.
"Low efficiency in the state sector is hampering the nation's industrial competitiveness," he said. "We will promote our privatisation programme strongly to sharpen the competitive edge."
On Friday the finance ministry announced it would shed its stake in several smaller concerns.

The government plans to sell its 46.8 percent stake in Korea Housing and Commercial Bank in 1997, depending on market conditions, a ministry statement said. The bank is capitalised at 235 billion won ($285 million).
"The plan to sell the government stake next year is firm. But the timing will be set to minimise adverse effects on the stock market," said a ministry official, who declined to be identified.
State-run Korea Telecom will also sell its 33.5 percent stake in Korea PC Telecom Co Ltd by 1998, the ministry said.
The ministry said it would try to sell the Korea PC stake the small- and mid-sized companies first, but if that fails it would widen the offer. Korea PC has paid-in capital of 20 billion won.
The government this year would seek to sell its 20.5 percent stake in Saehan Merchant Banking Corp held through the state-run Korea Development Bank, the statement said.
